lesson.title: Making Many Cables Act Like One: Link Aggregation
lesson.summary: Link aggregation combines multiple physical Ethernet connections into a single logical link, boosting aggregate capacity and adding failover, without changing how anything above it perceives the connection.
lesson.body:
A single Ethernet cable running at a fixed speed, say 1 Gbps, often becomes the bottleneck between a busy server and the rest of the network long before the switch or the server's own CPU runs out of headroom. Buying faster network cards and faster switch ports for every device that needs more throughput is expensive, and it does nothing about the more basic problem that one cable, one link, has a hard ceiling. Link aggregation solves this by taking several physical Ethernet links between the same two devices and binding them into one logical connection, so everything above them, the operating system, the switching fabric, any application, sees a single fast pipe instead of several separate ones.

The standard mechanism is the Link Aggregation Control Protocol, LACP, defined originally in IEEE 802.3ad and now folded into IEEE 802.1AX. Two devices, typically a server and a switch, or two switches, run LACP on a set of ports to automatically discover which physical links can be bundled, confirm both ends agree on the bundle, and continuously monitor link health. Because this builds directly on Ethernet, each physical link in the bundle still carries ordinary Ethernet frames with normal MAC addressing; LACP simply decides which physical link carries which frame.

That last point matters more than people expect. A link aggregation group does not make a single conversation go faster than one link allows. Instead, the switch or server uses a hashing function, commonly based on source and destination MAC address, IP address, or TCP or UDP port number, to decide which physical link within the bundle each traffic flow rides on. A given flow is pinned to one physical link for its entire lifetime, so that its packets cannot arrive out of order.

Consider a file server connected to a switch with four aggregated 1 Gbps links, forming a logical 4 Gbps LACP bundle. If twenty employees each pull files at modest speed, the hashing algorithm spreads their twenty separate flows fairly evenly across the four physical links, and the server can genuinely push close to 4 Gbps in aggregate. But if one employee tries to copy a single enormous file over one TCP connection, that flow hashes to exactly one of the four links and is capped near 1 Gbps, no matter how idle the other three links are. Link aggregation adds aggregate capacity across many conversations, not raw speed to any single one.

The other major benefit is resilience. If one of the four cables in that example fails or gets unplugged, LACP detects the loss within seconds and stops sending traffic on that link, redistributing affected flows across the three that remain. The logical connection stays up throughout, just at reduced capacity, which is why link aggregation is standard practice between core switches and on connections to servers where an outage is costly. It pairs naturally with the underlying communication link concept: aggregation combines several individually imperfect physical links into one connection with better aggregate throughput and better fault tolerance than any single link could offer alone.
